Empirical network analysis, as reviewed so far, contributes to the existing theoretical
results on systemic risk in the interbank market by considering the overall structure
of the network (thus going beyond the earlier focus on its degree of completeness,
as illustrated in Figure .). It also provides a stronger basis for the assessment
of contagion risk by means of counterfactual simulations. Counterfactual simulation
models often have roots in various percolation and cascade models developed within
statistical mechanics and network theory. One branch of this literature has investigated
the resilience of processes in different network topologies in terms of a connectivity
(orpercolation)threshold(examplesareshownbyBollobas,MooreandNewman
, and Callaway et al. ) at which a network dissolves into several disconnected
components. A well-known finding is that scale-free networks are more robust to
random failures than other types of networks, although they are very susceptible to the
removal of the very few highly connected nodes. However, such static failure models
aremoreapplicabletonetworksinwhichtheinterestistheavailabilityofpathsbetween
nodesinthenetwork(e.g.,intransportation)butarelessapplicabletonetworksofmon-
etaryflowsthatcontainbothflowsviatheshortestpathsaswellasanywalkswithinthecomputational models of financial networks 429
network. Anotherbranchoftheliteraturehasstudiedtheimpactofperturbationsthat
cascade through the network on the basis of established theoretical or domain-specific
rules (see Sachtjen et al.  and Kinney et al.  for power networks). In these
dynamic models nodes generally have a capacity to operate at a certain load and, once
the threshold is exceeded, some or all of the node’s load is distributed to neighboring
nodes in the network. While the detailed dynamics depend on the rules applied for the
cascades, generally the most connected nodes (or nodes with highest load in relation
to overall capacity) are more likely than an average node to trigger cascades.
Cascade models have been applied to various systems in fields such as geology,
biology, and sociology, as shown by Jensen (). This research has demonstrated
that models made of very simple agents, interacting with neighboring agents, can yield
surprising insights about system-level behavior. Models applied to financial systems
havebeendevelopedby,forexample,Nieretal.(),whoalsousesimulatedexposure
data, and Bastos e Santos and Cont (), who use data from the Brazilian credit
registry. Others (Lorenz et al. ; Georg ) have applied cascade models to
systemic risk analysis. Recently Battiston et al. () proposed the DebtRank metric
to quantify the systemic importance of banks. DebtRank is based on the structure
of an exposure network and represents the proportion of the network’s total value
that could be affected by distress or default in a given bank. Aldasoro and Angeloni
() develop six indicators that capture different aspects of systemic importance.
Acemoglu et al. () provide a new framework for studying the relation between the
financial network architecture and the likelihood of systemic failures due to contagion
of counterparty risk.
Craig and von Peter () introduce the concept of a core-periphery, or tiered,
structure for banking systems. The concept entails a small group of highly connected
core banks and a larger group of less-connected periphery banks. Many central banks
and researchers have since applied their methodology, for example, in pursuit of
identifying a set of systemically important banks. A core-periphery system has the
following properties:
• Core banks lend to each other.
• Periphery banks do not lend to each other.
• Core banks lend to (some) periphery banks.
• Core banks borrow from (some) periphery banks.
Real banking systems deviate somewhat from this perfect core-periphery structure,
some by having core banks not linked to all other core banks some by having links
between periphery banks. Nevertheless, the core-periphery concept has proven useful
for understanding markets and banking systems and for identifying important banks.
Forexample,CraigandvonPeter()findacore-peripherystructureintheGerman
banking system and also find that bank-level features such as connectedness and

The finding that large, well-connected banks are more likely to be in the core lends
support to the core-periphery structure as a realistic model for banking systems. Craig
and von Peter also find that the core-periphery classification of banks in the German
system is stable over time; Fricke and Lux () report similar findings for the e-MID
trading platform, and Langfield et al. () report a core-periphery structure in the
UK interbank system.
A rich literature examining interbank exposure networks has emerged in recent
years. While each network of interbank exposures is different, common features have
been uncovered. In order to simplify the complex network structure and dynamics,
theliteraturehasrecentlydevelopedmetricsthatsummarizeinformationaboutaspects
that are important to policy. In other fields where network models have been used, the
centrality of nodes has been an active area of research for decades. The new metrics
and algorithms particularly suited for interbank networks to identify systemically
important banks or sets of banks are based on cascade models and the identification
of core-periphery structures.
14.4 Correlation Networks .............................................................................................................................................................................
Today there is a focus on how network theory can be used to explain and better
understand financial markets. A main area is the study of correlation-based networks.
These networks can be used to reduce the complexity of financial dependencies, to
enhance the understanding of dynamics in financial markets, and to identify market
anomalies and outliers.
AseminalpaperisMantegna(),whichdevelopsamethodologyforrepresenting
asset correlations as trees. The paper introduces a method for extracting a subgraph
(asset tree) of the most relevant links from a complex network, where links represent
observed correlations between asset prices and returns. By constructing the minimum
spanning tree (MST) Mantegna finds that the U.S. stocks are grouped on the basis of
their industry sectors. Onnela et al. () introduce a new network type known as the
dynamic asset graph. This is similar to the asset tree introduced by Mantegna (),
but the function for mapping correlations into link lengths (the distance function)
is nonlinear. Like MSTs, dynamic asset graphs have N– links in total (where N =
number of nodes); however, in a dynamic asset graph the links may form loops, and
unconnected nodes are allowed.

can identify clusters, such as a cluster on the right with many Scandinavian currencies.
For a more in-depth study on correlations of currency returns, see Naylor et al. ().
Bonanno et al. () consider how the returns of stocks traded in a market are
affectedbyvaryingthetimehorizonsusedtocomputethecorrelationcoefficients.They
find that as the time horizon decreases the graph structure progressively changes from
a complex organization to a simple form (where clusters are sparser). The paper also
discusses volatility time series of stock prices and global financial markets.
A problem with MSTs is that they are very fragile to small changes in underlying
correlations. Tumminello et al. () extracts a subgraph of the most relevant links
from a complex network using the correlation coefficient matrix and Gower’s ()
metric distance. The paper outlines the method for constructing an MST and then
directly builds from this a planar maximally filtered graph (PMFG, as illustrated in
Figure .). The main constraint in the construction of an MST is that each new link
must not form a cycle, whereas a PMFG is a slightly more complex graph that allows
loopsandcliquesofuptofourelements.Itcanbedrawnonaplanarsurfacewithoutlink
crossings, and it is more robust to small changes in underlying correlations. The paper
develops MSTs and PMFGs of U.S. stock correlations and also considers the economic
properties of the four-clique structures in the PMFGs.
Another approach is taken by Kennet et al. (), who analyze stationary cor-
relations between stocks and introduce a new tool to investigate the structure and
dynamics of the market through the study of correlations. Financial markets are often
driven by common factors resulting in correlations between two assets that are driven432 kimmo soramäki

by a dependency on a third asset, or on the market in general. Kennet et al. ()
discuss the use of partial correlations (the correlation between two variables adjusted
for their relation with other variables) when studying correlation-based networks.
A partial correlation network can be used as a tool for filtering the most relevantcomputational models of financial networks 433
dependencies between assets. The PMFG is adapted so that it can be constructed from
partial correlations to form a partial correlation planar maximally filtered graph. The
paperalsogivesdetailsonconstructingthepartialcorrelationthresholdnetwork,atype
ofdependencynetworkinwhichtheinclusionoflinksdependsonmeansandstandard
deviations of nodes. All methods are demonstrated on stock data from the New York
Stock Exchange.
Correlations measure an unobserved link that may be caused by a multitude of
underlying factors. As such they are very different from the links normally considered
by network analysis, which are observed and measured rather than inferred. On the
other hand, correlation networks are quite flexible and can be constructed from any
time-series data to uncover linkages.
14.5 Concluding Remarks .............................................................................................................................................................................
This section provides some views concerning how financial network research can be
further operationalized to become policy and what challenges lie ahead.
Payment system research has been an area of financial research in which simulation
and network models were applied first, probably because data of the necessary
granularity has long been available from interbank payment systems. Results gained
in this field have also, in some cases, been used to argue for regulatory change in
others (see, e.g., Lo ). Better data about other infrastructures and markets will
allow regulators to develop more complete maps of the financial system. These maps
will be invaluable for decision support of crisis management, when time is too short
to develop more robust models and when intuition can be assisted by data mining.
Financial network analysis and network visualizations are likely to be good tools for
gaining this intuition and for developing more objective network-based metrics. The
challenge for regulators is to develop systems that allow the monitoring of the financial
system over time—ideally, in real time. Financial relationships are in a continuous flux
and can rapidly change form in the event of a financial crisis.
Sincethe–financialcrisis,thearchitectureoffinancialregulationhasbeen
subject to an overhaul. Within financial regulation, systemic risk is currently being
addressedbyenhancingmacroprudentialsupervision,andmanysupervisorshavebeen
mandated to carry out systemic risk monitoring. New systemic risk regulators such
as the Office of Financial Research in the United States and the European System of
Financial Supervisors have been set up.
Two policy innovations agreed on by the G are particularly noteworthy from the
aspect of networks. First, the G agreed that systemically important banks should be
subjecttoadditionalcapitalrequirements.Higherrequirementsforlossabsorbencyfor
importantnodesshouldreducetheriskthatcontagionpropagatesthroughthenetwork
of interbank exposures. Second, the G agreed that all standardized over-the-counter434 kimmo soramäki
(OTC) derivative contracts should be traded on exchanges or electronic trading plat-
forms, where appropriate, and cleared through central counterparties. Central clearing
of derivative contracts should reduce the quantity of counterparty risk, information
asymmetry, and complexity in the financial system.
These policy innovations also give rise to research challenges in the field of financial
networks.First,theBaselCommittee’smethodology()foridentifyingsystemically
importantbanksdoesnotincorporaterequirementsormodelsbasedoninformationon
bilateralexposures.Suchdatais,however,alreadycollectedbymanyregulatorswhoare
developingmethodologiesthatmakeuseofthismoregranulardata.Second,mandatory
clearing of OTC derivatives potentially increases the systemic importance of central
counterparties.Investigatingthispossibleunintendedconsequenceshouldbeapriority
for research on financial networks.
Before the financial crisis of –, regulators had little access to network data
beyond the payment system. As a consequence of the crisis they have much broader
mandates to collect data and as a consequence are facing the opposite challenge: the
management and summarization of large data sets. In this context, researchers should
continue to develop methods to summarize voluminous data in accurate and econom-
ically meaningful ways. This includes improvements to visualizations of complex data,
which would allow policy makers to view systemic vulnerabilities in real time.
A rapidly developing area of current financial network research is based on corre-
lation networks. Using data reduction algorithms, large correlation matrices can be
filtered to produce simpler networks that still retain much relevant information and
allow quicker visual identification of the main dependence structures. Various degrees
ofdatareductionarepossible.Forexample,theminimumspanningtree,presentingthe
bare minimum, can be modified to form the planar maximally filtered graph, which
includes more links and also cliques, without displaying the full complex network.
Information-theoretically better methods based on the use of partial correlations
and statistical models instead of graph theoretic concepts are also being developed.
Correlation networks summarize and can visually display vast amounts of market
information and together with new algorithms for outlier and regime detection give
regulators easier access to the information-processing capabilities of the market.
Tools for network analysis have improved substantially over the past few years, and
many open-source projects and tools are available for free for research purposes. The
main general-purpose tools for network analysis include Pajek (Batagelj and Mrvar
)andGephi(Bastianetal.).TheiGraph(CsardiandNepusz)libraryfor
the statistical software R (R Development Core Team ) contains many algorithms
for analyzing complex networks. These programs contain some visualization modules.
For more advanced programming needs, JavaScript libraries like d.js (Bostock et al.
) and Sigma.js (http://simgajs.org) provide the needed flexibility. The application
of network analysis to monitor and assess systemic risk and contagion in financial
systems should benefit from important progress made in other sciences. Keep in mind,
however, that the results depend on the process and behavior of the particular network
andmaynotbedirectlyapplicabletothefinancialcontext.Anonlineanalyticsplatformcomputational models of financial networks 435
implementingmanyofthecentralityalgorithmsandvisuallayoutssuitableforfinancial
networksisFNA(FinancialNetworkAnalytics,www.fna.fi;SoramäkiandCook).
In addition to mapping the financial system at a given point in time, researchers and
policy makers need to take into account the mechanics of the financial system in order
to be able to make informed forecasts of likely courses of events. These mechanics have
becomemorecomplexandautomatedwithcontinuousadvancesintechnology.Human
decision making, and therefore economic behavior, is in many cases pre-programmed
as algorithms and, as a consequence bounded not only by rationality but also by
the operational IT framework. Modern financial systems involve a high degree of
automation both in how decisions are made and how they are executed, including
algorithmictrading,straight-throughprocessingofsettlement,andautomatedrulesfor
liquidity management of the settlement process. These automated infrastructures have
become ubiquitous but are not well understood. For example, under stressed market
conditions the automated execution of trades can trigger extreme price movements,
and the interactions between automated orders and algorithmic trading strategies can
be unpredictable—and once the rules have been set up they are part of the system
mechanics. The system is highly complex and, even in the absence of any human
decisionmaking,exhibitsmanyfeedbackloopsthataffectperformance.Counterfactual
simulations, as developed for payment systems and contagion of interbank exposures,
can bring improved understanding of the interaction of the mechanics of a system.
In spite of larger amounts of data and better ways to summarize and use it as a
basis for computational economic and financial models, financial networks will likely
be limited to providing views of the functioning of particular subsystems of the whole
economy.Theinterdependenciesbetweennetworkedsystems(multilayernetworks)are
only very recently being considered by researchers. Also, network models will likely
serverelativelywellforunderstandingtheconsequencesofsystemicevents,andwillbe
somewhat limited for foreseeing their occurrence, because they suffer from the same
limitation(accessonlytohistoricaldataaboutrareevents)asdootherempiricalmodels.
Overall, network-based methods that take into account the complex connections in
the financial system and allow for their visual presentation in intuitive ways will
help the industry, regulators, and researchers better understand financial markets and
infrastructures.

15.1 Introduction .............................................................................................................................................................................
It is probably not an exaggeration to say that the theory of rational expectations really
is at the very core, hiding deep down in the framework, of most theories used in
finance since the mid-s. The idea is very simple and very elegant, and has very
deep implications.
Unfortunately, it is also very unrealistic. This chapter aims to go beyond such a
traditional view of finance but also beyond the more recent behavioral finance view,
which as its starting point takes the case of individual investor psychology. The main
themewillbepriceformationinfinancialmarkets,seenasasociologicalphenomenon.
For a background on the ideas presented here, see Andersen and Nowak ().
Ifwerejectthethemainbuildingblockoffinancialmodels,therationalexpectations
hypothesis, as unrealistic, the undeniable question is then, How can we do better? The
lack of established and convincing alternatives is probably one of the main reasons
why macroeconomists keep on using rational expectations in their models, for the
simple fear of the “wilderness” of alternatives. If we are not to use the sharply defined
hypothesis of rational expectations, then what exactly do we use?
## 15.1.1 Chaos Theory and Financial Markets
One of the main issues with rational expectations theory is the assumption that all
investors act alike, analyzing the market in a cool and pervasive manner by using all
available information relevant to future cash flows of a given asset. This description
sounds far from reality, and is far from reality, as probably most economists would442 jorgen vitting andersen
agree. Let us instead for one moment take the extreme opposite view. Assume for
a moment, in a thought experiment, that we know all investors, their wealth, and
their investment strategies independent of the condition of the markets. Let us also
assume that we were somehow able to put this huge amount of information into a
fast supercomputer. Would we then able to understand and predict future market
movements?
This line of thinking goes back to the tradition from Pierre Simon de Laplace, a
French scientist born in the eighteenth century, who in his book A Philosophical Essay
on Probabilities” () wrote:
We may regard the present state of the universe as the effect of the past and cause of
the future. An intellect which at any given moment knew all the forces that animate
nature and the mutual positions of the beings that compose it, if this intellect was
vast enough to submit the data to analysis, could condense into a single formula the
movement of the greatest bodies of the universe and that of the lightest atom; for
such an intellect nothing could be uncertain and the future just like the past would
be present before its eyes.
OnecenturylateracompatriotofLaplace’s,HenriPoincaré,woulddiscoverthathaving
just the equations is not enough since we also need to know the initial conditions
of a system in exact detail: given the slightest change in initial conditions, the same
equations could give completely different results. With the invention of computers and
the computing power they obtained in the s, it became possible to formalize this
point and now name it “chaos theory.” Most readers probably will recognize chaos
theory because of the meteorologist Edward Lorenz, who coined the saying that the
flap of a butterfly’s wings in Brazil sets off a tornado in Texas.
Let us, then, step back and reconsider the question posed two paragraphs above
concerning the predictability of future market movements. We can summarize the
situation as follows According to rational expectations theory used in traditional
finance, financial market movements are random and consequently impossible to
predict, full stop! Laplace, on the other hand, opens up the exact opposite scenario
with everything in this universe described by determinism, from the movement of
an atom to that of a galaxy, and of course in between these two extremes, all other
activity including the movement of prices in a stock market. Even though Laplace’s
considerations are more philosophical in nature than of practical relevance, the idea is
that everything ultimately could be understood deterministically if we could just grasp
therightunderlyingvariablesgoverningallforcesinnatureandanalyzethepositionsof
beings in it. Poincaré agrees with the determinism in the equations but points out that
inpracticeunderstandingtheworlddeterministicallyisforeverbeyondourreachsince
changing the initial conditions of the equations changes their outcome. This, however,
hasnotheldpeoplebackfromtryingtounderstandingmarketmovementsusingchaos
theory, assuming some underlying variables governing cycles of price formation in
financial markets much as they do business cycles governing the economy. The goal in
that case is to determine a so-called strange attractor, or finding out which dimensionsfrom minority games to $-games 443
give the number of relevant variables in question. The principle of a parsimonious
description of a system in terms of some few underlying relevant variables is the
hallmarkofmosttheoriescomingfromthefieldofphysics,andithasprovedsuccessful
when imported to other domains such as bio-physics and geo-Physics. It is probably
fair to say that the jury is still out when it comes to the possibility of gaining insight by
describing financial markets or economic developments in terms of chaos theory. The
complexity approach to be presented in the following, rather than looking for some
equations with relevant variables, stresses the impact that each constituent can have on
asystem.Bytreatingeachconstituentofasystem,complexitytheoryinasenseappears
more “chaotic” than to chaos theory, which, instead of considering all the constituents,
only considers a few. If we return to the question of price formation in a financial
market, each constituent is an entity that takes part in making the price by trading,
be it a computer or a human. The question, then, is how to find order in this seeming
cacophony of voices of the constituents.
## 15.1.2 Complexity Theory and the “Symphony” of the Market
In order to visualize the complexity models to be introduced in the following, let us
for a moment try to make the analogy between the way that prices are formed in a
financialmarket,andthecreationofasymphonybyanorchestra.Onecanthinkofeach
marketparticipantasamusicianinsuchanorchestra,playingadifferenttunes(trading
frequency and direction of trade) with different volume (amount of cash behind a
trade). The role of the “maestro” that the market participants watch would be played
by the central bankers worldwide. The question is whether we are somehow able to
decode the symphony of price movements played by such an orchestra.
Eventhoughtheanalogymightsoundabitfar-fetched,itdoesillustratethecollective
behavior of a system in which humans have to perform an act that depends on
the outcome of what other people do. Just as different traders use different trading
strategies, so do different musicians in an orchestra have different sheet music that
they use in the act of playing. Sheet music tells the musician how to play, but he or
she has to wait for his or her colleagues to play the instrument in the right manner. It
is similar for decisions in a trading strategy played by a trader. A trader never acts in
complete isolation but takes his or her decisions depending on the“tune” played by the
market. Trend-following strategies depend on the momentum of the market, whereas
fundamental value strategies depend of the price level of the market; traders buy when
thestockhasbecomeundervaluedandsellingwhenthestockhasbecomeovervalued.
In addition, anticipation of how future tunes will be played matters because of new
policy making by central bankers or new economic statistics.
The complex but also fascinating, way the market symphony is created, becomes
clearer when we consider its hierarchical structure. At the first level of the hierarchy,
we can imagine each given stock and its price movements being played by a local444 jorgen vitting andersen
orchestra of individual traders. This local tune (price movements of the stock) is not
made in complete isolation but depends (in part) on the how other local orchestras
(other stocks) play their melodies. Going up one level, we can then consider the
tune-of-a-stock created by the aggregate action of traders, now itself as created by a
single instrument, but playing in a national orchestra composed of all stocks in an
index. Adding up the contributions of the local orchestras creates what one could call a
national hymn, illustrated by a given country’s stock index. As discussed in Andersen
et al. (), the hierarchical structure does not stop at the level of a given country,
but goes into a super-hierarchical structure where a global symphony is played by a
worldwide orchestraof allnationalities.Eachnationalorchestradoesnotplay itshymn
in isolation but has to wait for the outcome of the other orchestras in order to know
how the play its hymn properly.
## 15.1.3 Agent-Based Modeling: Search for Universality
Classes in Finance?
Havingdiscussedthewaythediversityinhumandecisionmakingcollectivelysomehow
creates a symphony of price movements, the question is, How one can formalize such
an image? One step in this direction is to use agent-based models which are built, so to
speak, to allow for diversity when it comes to decision making.
The concept of agent-based models dates from the s and the ideas of John von
Neumann and Stanislaw Ulam, who were interested in self-replicating machines and
came up with the idea of the cellular automata. Like cellular automata, agent-based
models cover a very broad range mostly computational models, that simulate the
actions and interactions of some set of autonomous entities called agents. With this
description the link to complex systems should be clear. In the context of finance and
economics the great advantage of agent-based models is that they give us a means to
introduce behavioral traits at the micro level of each agent, and then study how such
traitsandrulesofinteractionamongtheagentsgeneratecomplexbehavioratthesystem
level.
Originating in the domain of physics, several types of agent-basedmodels have been
proposedtodescribethedynamicsofpricinginfinancialmarkets.Typicallythesekinds
ofmodelsconsiderafinancialmarketascomposedofagentsthatusestrategiestobuyor
sell shares. The decision could, for example, be based on an estimation of fundamental
values or, in order to encompass technical analysis, based on the last price movements
of the market. The agents are flexible since they adapt to the price movements of the
market,choosingthemostsuccessfulstrategyateachtimestep.Inthisperspectivesuch
models offer a ground-breaking view of financial marketssince the agents are bounded
rational with, in some cases, exact solutions obtained via techniques borrowed from
physics.
Before going into the specifics of the different agent-based models, I begin with a
word of caution. It is easy to fall into the trap of considering narrowly each model as afrom minority games to $-games 445
completedescriptionofagivenfinancialmarket.Clearlynomodelwilleveraccomplish
thefulltaskofexplainingineverydetailthepricedynamicsofafinancialmarket,justas
nomapevercantellalldetailsofalocation.Still,mapsareusefulforgettinganoverview,
and my claim in the following is similarly that we need models to guide us through
the wilderness of the price dynamics of financial markets. I would rather emphasize a
view in which the models serve as probes or handles used to get a successively better
descriptions of what one could call “generic” behavior of financial markets. Generic
behavior could, for example, be the point of identifying certain moments when the
markets are framed, as discussed below. Let us stress realism as the main advantage
of the complexity models compared to the traditional rational expectations models.
We know from psychology that people do not behave rationally (Kahneman ).
Incorporating nonrationality via complexity models therefore appears as an appealing
alternative to models based on the rational expectations hypothesis.
At the lowest level of description, a complexity model of a financial market could be
defined as follows: “A financial market is a place where a number of actors trade, using
different strategies.” Even though this statement does not say a lot, it is hard to dispute,
and it can serve as a foundation for what follows. The fear of traditional economists
is, however, that this will never bring us very far, since the next refinement in such a
description can be taken in an infinite number of different directions.
Physics faced what at first appeared to be somewhat similar concerns in the s,
s, and s. The question then was, How much detail is really needed to describe
a given system properly? This question is relevant also in the present context, since if
a detailed description of the price dynamics of a financial market is needed with all
its interwoven facets, then there will not be much hope of gaining insight on financial
markets using the rather simple models introduced below. It is, however, noteworthy
thattheproblemsencounteredinphysicseventuallyledtothedevelopmentoftoolsnow
used in different areas of physics that go under the general name of “renormalization
group theory.” Back then there were concerns in the domain of particle physics (atomic
physics) that in order to understand the interactions of the forces in nature one needed
a detailed description of the forces described at a certain scale (distance). It turns out
that, for example, an electron, which looks like a singular solid object when seen from
afar, looks differently as one zooms in. As one decreases the viewing distance (goes to
higher energies) an electron appears to be composed of self-similar copies of yet other
electrons,positrons,andphotons.Similarlyastockindexisn’tjustastockindexbuthas
its own life in terms of the stocks that constitutes it. Also the forces that acts between
different stock indices appear different than the forces acting between the individual
stocks.
The development of the renormalization group theory was the result of successive
contributions. First Stueckelberg and Petermann (), then Gell-Mann and Low
(), followed by Feynman, Schwinger and Tomonaga (who won the Nobel Prize
in physics in  for their contribution) showed how details, depending on scale,
were irrelevant. A deeper understanding of this problem came from condensed matter
physics (Kadanoff ; Wilson ), the technique was used to understand the446 jorgen vitting andersen
generalnatureofphasetransitions.ThisledtoyetanotherNobelPrize,illustratinghow
important the technique has become in modern physics.
The lesson from physics tells us that insight can be gained as one studies how forces
change when varying the typical scale of a phenomenon. The question is whether
similarinsightcouldbeusedinunderstandinghowmarketforceschange,wheninstead
of looking at correlations between different stocks in an index, one goes to a different
scaleandconsiderstheforcesactingnowbetweendifferentstockindices,withcurrency
and commodity indices adding complexity to such an understanding. In a similar vein,
itwouldbeinterestingtohaveatheoreticalunderstandingofhowmarketforceschange
asonechangethetimescaleinquestion,relatingeventsatthetimescaleofsecondsand
minutes to what happens at the hourly, daily and monthly time scale. I mention this in
part because use of an analogy to gain insight into market forces by looking at what
happens when one changes the scale is appealing, but, more important, because the
renormalization group theory explains the concept of “universality” seen in physical
systems. It turns out that phase transitions seen in, for example, magnetic systems,
alloy materials, and superfluid and superconducting transitions, despite their apparent
different nature, have similar critical exponents, meaning that near the transition
phase their behavior is identical. The phase transitions of these very different systems
can therefore all be described by the same set of relevant variables, leaving out (as
mentioned in the paragraph above) a detailed description for each system as irrelevant
to understanding the physics governing the phase transitions. It should be mentioned
that the notion of universality extends to systems that are out of equilibrium. In that
caseithasbeenshownhowdomaingrowthof,forexample,growingcrystals,orgrowth
of domains of oxygen in high-temperature superconductors, again is determined by a
few relevant variables (such as the dimensions of the system and whether the so-called
order parameter is conserved or not). Given the success of renormalization group
theory,physicistsarethereforebroughtuptolookfortherelevantvariablesofasystem,
knowing that details ultimately should not matter. It is through such a lens that the
modelsintroducedbelowshouldbeseen:asprimitivemodelsoffinancialmarketsthat,
despite their simplicity, are meant as probes to search for what could be the equivalent
of relevant variables in financial markets.

## 15.2.1 The El Farol Bar Game and the Minority Game
The El Farol Bar Game was invented by the economist Brian Arthur (Arthur ).
In the game N people have to decide independently each week whether go to at theirfrom minority games to $-games 447
favorite bar, which once a week has some very popular live folk music. The problem,
however, is that the bar only has L < N/ chairs. Now since each person will only
be happy if seated, the people try to use the past week’s attendance to predict future
attendance. If a person predicts that the number of people who will attend is larger
thanL,thatpersonwillstayhome.NoticethattheElFarolBarGamedescribesadaptive
behavior, since the audience in the bar uses past data to predict future attendance.
Onereasontodiscussthismodelisthatitgivesaclearexampleofasituationinwhich
rational expectations theory cannot be used to solve the problem. Suppose a rational
expectationspredictionmachineexistedandthatalltheagentspossessedacopyofit.If
the machine predicted, for instance, that a number larger than L would attend the bar,
nobody would show up, thereby negating the prediction of the machine.
InspiredbytheElFarolBarGame,Ye-ChengZhangandDamienChalletintroduced
the Minority Game (Challet and Zhang ) as an agent-based model proposed to
studymarketpricedynamics.Themodelfollowsaleadingprincipleinphysics,namely,
thatinordertosolveacomplexproblemoneshouldfirstidentifyessentialfactorsatthe
expense of trying to describe all aspects in detail. The Minority Game (MG) therefore
should be considered as a minimal model of a financial market. It is described by just
three parameters:
• N, the number of agents (market participants)
• mi, the memory of agent i
• si, the number of strategies available to agent i
in the case where all agents use the same memory mi ≡ m and the same number of
strategiessi ≡s(tobeassumedinthefollowing).ThenameMinorityGamewasinspired
by the El Farol Bar Game; the agents are rewarded whenever their decision is in the
minority. I explain this point in detail below where I define the payoff function.

the last m directional moves of the market. Representing an upward movement of

ThemainproblemwiththeMinorityGameis,ofcourse,thatitishardtoimaginepeople

People trade either because they try to make money or because they need to hedge

MinorityGame,andthiswasthemaincriticismthatleadtoanotheragent-basedmodel,

Iwouldliketoadvocateforwhatcouldbebestbecalledascientificapproachtofinance.
Scientific, because researchers propose experiments to go hand in hand with theory, a
traditionthatcomesfromthehardsciencesbutisarareapproachintraditionalfinance.
Ithasbeenarguedthatthereasonforthesuccessofthehardsciencesispreciselythelink
betweenproposingtheoriesormodelsagainstwhichonecantestviaexperiments.This
liesattheheartofthephilosophyofsciencesuggestedbytheAustro-Britishphilosopher
Karl Popper (–). He introduced the idea that a scientific theory can never
be completely verified no matter how many times experimental testing confirms the
assumptions of the theory, but one single case in which the theory is shown not to
holdexperimentally,canfalsifythetheory.Theterm“falsifiable,”introducedbyPopper,
simply means that if a theory is wrong one should be able to show this by experiments.
By the same logic this also means that if somebody introduces a theory that cannot be
falsified it is not a scientific theory. The efficient market hypothesis is an example of a
theory that can never be falsified by experiments, and therefore in Popper’s view, is not
ascientifictheory.Popperplacedfalsifiabletheoriesattherootoftheapparentprogress
of scientific knowledge over time, and therefore they also seem like the best candidates
for a way forward in finance.
Having stressed the need for experiments according to Popper, it is noteworthy that
experimental finance took a big step forward with the awarding of the Nobel Prize in
economics to Vernon Smith in . His most significant work was concerned with
market mechanisms and tests of different forms of auction. By far the major part
of the experimental work in finance (including that by Vernon Smith), however, has
consideredhumanrationalityandtheabilityofmarketstofindtheproperpricecloseto
anequilibriumsetting.Contrarytothisapproach,behavioralfinanceusesamuchmore
realistic description of how actual decision making takes place in financial markets.
It would therefore seem like a very natural approach to take the insight gained from
behavioral finance and apply it to experiments performed on financial markets.
Very little effort has been made in this direction. The main reason is may be that

Game or the -Game. In this formalism, cognitive closure is defined as the decoupling
of an agent’s strategies from the market feedback.
In what follows I describe decoupling in the context of the G but should note that
this is a general property related to agent-based games that use look-up tables like
table..Itisimportantfortheunderstandingofthefollowingtonotethattheoptimal
state of the G is the solution in which the price deviates exponentially in time from
the fundamental value of the asset, enabling all agents to profit from constant price
increases or decreases in the bubble or anti-bubble states. Finding the optimal solution
in the G requires coordination among the agents to enter and stay in such states.
Coordination,however,isnotdrivenbyintentionallycooperativebehaviorofallagents;
rather,it emergesfromindependentdecisionsofthemajorityofagentswhochoosethe
optimal strategies from the entire set of strategies. These optimal strategies, presented
in the reference tables, happen to lead to the same action, which on an aggregate level
is seen as synchronization. The question is whether this mathematical formalism can
adequately describe the process of human decision making.
Agents’ strategies, at first glance, are very different from what we know about
decision heuristics of humans (Tversky and Kahneman ). Decision heuristics
providerulesforhumandecisionmaking.Heuristicsareformedintermsofverbally(or
rather propositionally) formulated conditional rules. Clearly, humans are cognitively
incapable of precisely representing the many vectors and exact sequences of market
dynamics needed to represent and valuate the strategies. The reverse formalization of
human decision heuristics by lookup tables is simple, however. Any conditional rule of
humanreasoningcanberepresentedbyalookuptable.Inordertoacceptthenotionthat
agents’strategiesrepresenthumandecisionheuristics,weonlyneedtoassumethateach
agent’s strategy depicts in an algorithmic way implementation of a decision heuristic
that for humans would be specified in higher-level language.
In this vein, cognitive closure in market players may be interpreted as setting up the
mindforwhatwillhappeninrelativelydistantfuture,regardlessofwhathappensinthe
near future. In terms of decision heuristics, after observing certain patterns of market
dynamicsinvestorsmaycometotheconclusionthatthemarkettrendissetand,further,
thetemporarymarketreversalsarenotindicativeoftherealmarkettrend.Forexample,from minority games to $-games 459
if the market player judges that the market trend is upward, then the increase in price
serves as a confirmation of the expected trend, so the decision is to buy. A drop in
price may be perceived as a momentary deviation from the governing trend, which
indicates immediate correction, so the decision is also to buy. This may be translated as
decoupling of agents’ strategies, something that will be crucial in understanding how
speculative bubbles are formed.
As long as the majority of investors are reacting to incoming information the market
dynamicisunpredictable.If,however,alargeenoughproportionofinvestorsmakesthe
same decision about the direction, the market will evolve regardless of what happens
next.Themarketmaybecometemporarilypredictablesinceinvestorsareinfactlocked
into their decisions, which are temporarily decoupled from information concerning
the market. A prolonged locked-in decision of investors to buy results in bubbles, and
locking in the decision to sell will result in market crashes.
Some strategies represented by reference tables have a unique property: the actions
that they recommend are decoupled from the incoming information. A decoupling of
thestrategymeansthatthedifferentpatternsofmarkethistoryleadtothesamedecision
(e.g., to buy), regardless of whether the market went up or down at the previous time
step.Themaininterestinthemechanismofdecouplingis,aswewillsee,thatitgivesus
a way to predict formation of speculative bubbles before they are seen in the price data.
## 15.3.2 The Formalism of Decoupling

At first it might seem like a somewhat theoretical exercise to predict ahead of
time how agents in a computer simulation will behave. One could argue that since
the setup of the computer program is entirely determined by the parameters of the
simulations, all information is already encoded in the program, and the only thing
needed to predict movement two time steps ahead would be to let the program run
two additional steps and then see what happened. This suggestion, however, misses
the point concerning the more interesting situations of practical applications where
simulations of the agent-based models are “locked” to real market data, as explained in
section .. This corresponds to considering real predictions in real time. In the case
of applying real market data as input to the computer simulations of the agent-based
models, we encounter the situation of knowing, for example, the closure of the markets
today.Observingamomentofdecouplinginthecomputersimulationsgiventhemarket
closure of today means that we know what the agent-based model will predict, not for
tomorrow, but for the day after tomorrow. In that case we don’t need to wait and see
how the markets close tomorrow to be able to make the prediction tomorrow—it can
be made today.

Having glimpsed how to apply the idea behind decoupling to real data, we now turn
our attention to the detection of speculative financial bubbles. The following section
will give additional insight into when decoupling could be a mechanism driving real
price dynamics, and in particular, under which circumstances this mechanism could
be used in the prediction of the onset of speculative bubbles.

15.4 Conclusions .............................................................................................................................................................................
I have tried to argue for uses of game theory and agent-based modeling that go beyond
thestandardmethodsusedintraditionalapproachestofinance.Theideaisthatweneed
models that more realistically describe the decision making of investors in financial
markets. Two such models have been introduced, the Minority Game and the -Game,
and their main results have been discussed. It has been argued that a more scientific
approach to finance is needed, with theories and with experiments carried out on
trading floors to falsify and thereby select relevant properties of theoretical models.
Some preliminary results in this direction have been shown by the introduction of the
idea of decoupling of investor decision making. The hope is that the present article can
helpsparkinterestinsuchascientificapproachtofinancewiththeintroductionofmore
models that can be tested by experiments performed on trading floors.

16.1 Introduction .............................................................................................................................................................................
Since  a team of academics from the University of Liverpool, City University of
New York, and the University of Melbourne have run the annual CAT Market Design
Tournament,orCATCompetition.Thiscompetition,whichispartofthelargerTrading
AgentsCompetition(TAC),aimstoencourageresearchintothedesignandapplication
of automated market mechanisms that are able to adapt to changing competitive
environments.
In computer science, there are many research areas where experimental platforms
have been developed for comparing and benchmarking research, and open competi-
tions have been built around some of these platforms. Examples include the MiniZinc
competition for finite domain constraint solvers and the various TAC competitions
for automated trading, supply-chain networks, online ad exchanges, and brokerage
of electric power. From the TAC competitions, the research arising on automated
trading, price prediction, and adaptive bidding has been summarized in the book by
Wellman et al. (). Perhaps the most famous series of research competitions in
computer science is Robocup, which since  has organized annual competitions
for soccer-playing robots, in separate leagues comprising physical robots of various

See http://www.minizinc.org/challenge.html.

See https://www.sics.se/projects/trading-agent-competition.the cat market design competition 469
shapes and sizes, as well as virtual players and managers. This crowd-sourced series
hasgeneratednofewerthannineteenannualvolumesofrefereedresearchpapers,each
published in Springer’s Lecture Notes in Computer Science series, as well as numerous
other publications, and advanced computer science considerably.
TheTRECconferenceoninformationretrieval isanotherexampleofacompetition
and online repository, in this case aimed at encouraging and comparing research into
information retrieval. This annual competition, started in the early s, aims to
promote research into a range of information retrieval tasks and provides sets of data
for researchers to use. However, work from Armstrong et al. () casts doubt on
the success of the TREC tournaments. Their research shows that the baselines used
in information retrieval experiments are typically uncompetitive in many cases they
perform worse than the first TREC experimental systems—and there is no upward
trend in scores, with results reported in  showing no improvement over results
from , and many  scores falling below the median of the original TREC
experimental systems. Entrants are not requested to upload their entries, as they are
in the CAT competition.
The aim of this chapter is to present our experience with the CAT competition
(section .), to present details of research that has arisen from the tournaments
(section .), and to evaluate whether the CAT competition has helped improve the
state of the art in automated mechanism design (section .), so that research in this
area does not go the way of information retrieval. To evaluate the CAT competition,
we experimentally compared the five annual winning entrants of the competition
(–) against each other in a series of five-player experiments, as well as a
series of two-player round-robin experiments. The results indicate that later entrants
performbetteronaggregate,especiallyinthefive-playerexperiments.Inthetwo-player
round-robin experiments, the most notable improvement came from the winner in the
second year of the competition, which was the first year that entrants had access to a
previous year’s entrants to run their own experiments.
16.2 The CAT Tournament .............................................................................................................................................................................
## 16.2.1 Motivation
The economic world we inhabit has an enormous diversity of marketplaces. From
garage sales of unwanted household goods to local bodegas and corner stores, to
supermarkets and international chains, through automated online exchanges for the
trading of complex derivative and futures products, this diversity is astonishing. The
response of mainstream economic theory to this diversity until recently, however,
was to abstract all the particular features of markets away to create a generic model,

See http://www.robocup.org/.

See http://trec.nist.gov/.470 tim miller et al.
a model of a marketplace having independent buyers and sellers who interact in a
uniform manner (which is often left implicit). This generic model ignores many of
the specific features of particular markets, for example, that in markets for medical
services, the provider and the purchase decision maker may often be the same person
(e.g., a doctor acting on behalf of a patient), or that in higher-education markets, the
consumer—the student—may also constitute the product being purchased, or that in
management consultancy markets, there may be no way for the purchaser to assess
the quality of the provided service, neither ahead of time nor even afterwards. Most
important, a generic model also abstracts away from the “ecology” of all the different
markets operating in broad parallel with one another, some competing directly with
others, some competing indirectly, some parasitic on others, some complementary to
others, and some generating information used by others (Mirowski ). Ignoring
this ecology of markets means that, for example, with a single generic model of a
marketplace we cannot explain why the world’s most sophisticated futures trading
exchanges in Chicago or New York or London operate within only short walking
distances from local household garage sales, and yet use very different rules and
procedures. Of course, such complex futures markets usually target different trading
participants than do garage sales, but this is precisely why the rules of the two types
of markets are different. A generic model of all markets does not allow for different
marketstohavedifferentrules,nordoesitseektounderstandtheimpactsanddynamics
of these rules and how they may interact with one another.
Although mainstream economics has long studied some exceptions to the generic
model of perfect competition—for example, monopoly, oligopoly, and monopsony
markets—the discipline has mostly ignored competition between marketplaces. But
competitionbetweenmarketshasgrowninimportancewiththeriseoftheInternet,the
Web, and electronic trading. While there are some exceptions in economic theory that
analyze competition between platforms, such as Ellison et al. () and Armstrong
(), the abstract nature of these models makes them unable to capture some
important, finer-level details of particular marketplace designs that have a major
influence on the emergent behavior of the market as a whole. With buyers, sellers, and
trading platforms now able to be located anywhere, so too may their transactions take
placeanywhere.Asaresult,thepreciserulesandproceduresofaparticularmarketmay
have important consequences for the attraction and retention of buyers or sellers, with
each trader able to choose between multiple competing marketplaces, and with each
marketplace having its own institutional rules and architecture.
Mirowski () argues that markets are fundamentally collections of diverse,
evolvingalgorithmsandthatthefieldofcomputerscienceisrequiredifwearetobetter
represent the complexity of economic processes in order to understand markets. We
believe that this is true for studying competition between heterogeneous marketplaces.
One keymotivation,therefore,for establishingthe CAT MarketDesignTournament
was to use computational simulations involving such algorithms to better understand
the nature of competition between heterogeneous marketplaces, in the absence of
any mature economic theories on this topic. In particular, such an understanding
should provide scientific knowledge and guidance on how specific market rules andthe cat market design competition 471
procedureswouldimpactmarketandtraderperformance,andhowtheywouldinteract
with or influence one another via competing markets. For example, Cai et al. ()
ran experiments using JCAT that restricted traders from moving between markets
that are somehow “connected” to neighboring marketplaces. Their results indicate
that the specific network topology of connections between marketplaces influences
the allocation of traders to marketplaces and the amount of time it takes to find an
equilibrium point. It is likely that the network topology between markets enforcing
other constraints, such as allowing exchange of information (e.g., unfilled orders or
fee structures), would also affect marketplace and trader actions and performance. The
operators of, and traders in, the world’s stock exchanges have anecdotal understanding
of these relationships and impacts, but no coherent, grounded, and granular theory
exists for the specific rules that exchange operators typically consider and deploy. Such
atheorywouldprovideguidancetothedesigners,implementers,andmanagersofelec-
tronicmarketplaces,peoplewhoareincreasinglyinformationtechnologistsratherthan
economists.
Second, given the rise of electronic trading and the globalization of trading, it is easy
to imagine that operators of exchanges would need to respond in real time, or close
to it, to changes in their business environments: If a competing exchange introduces
a new rule or new fee structure and quickly attracts more traders or traders who are
more desirable, then rival exchanges that are losing customers will need to respond as
quickly as possible. Thus, our second key motivation was to develop the science and
softwareengineeringofadaptivemarketmechanismdesign,aimingultimatelyforfully
automated mechanism design.
Traditionally, the design of market mechanisms has been undertaken by human
economists using a complex mix of mathematical analysis (chiefly using game the-
ory), computer simulation, experiments with human subjects, and trial operations.
Nik-Khah (), for example, observes that all of these methods were used in the
designof thespecificrules oftheU.S. FederalCommunicationsCommission’sauctions
of the PCS radio frequency spectrum in the mid-s. Given the subtlety and com-
plexity of actual market design engineering, it was not obvious how, or even whether,
automatedmarketmechanismdesignwouldbepossible.WedevelopedtheCATMarket
DesignTournamenttoencouragemultidisciplinaryresearchinthisareaandtoprovide
a standard experimental platform by which such research could be compared and

participants, our goal of encouraging research here has certainly been achieved, and
several promising approaches to adaptive and automated mechanism design proposed,
for example, Niu et al. (), Pardoe et al. (), and Phelps et al. ().
In designing the CAT Tournament and its supporting software platform JCAT,
we sought to model practice in actual (spot) financial exchanges, while keeping the
game rules straightforward. Thus, the marketplaces in CAT are called specialists,
representingthattheyarespecificagentsthattakeordersforparticularassets.Similarly,
the performance criteria used in the tournament reflect those used by managers to

counterparties). The strategies used by software traders in the JCAT platform are four

Full details of the organization of the CAT Market Design Tournament can be found

et al. ). In addition, the various research published by those involved in the CAT

## 16.2.2 Operation of the Tournament
We now briefly outline the structure of the CAT Tournament. Entrants to the
competition design and implement software agents, called specialists, which operate as
matchmakers between automated traders. In the JCAT platform, specialists represent
competing marketplaces in the same way that, say, the New York Stock Exchange,
NASDAQ, the London Stock Exchange, the Paris Bourse, and others all compete. The
traders,adaptivesoftwareagentsprovidedbythetournamentorganizers,buyandsella
singlegenericcommodity.Tradersareeitherbuyersorsellersbutnotboth.Eachtrading
day, each trader first selects a specialist to trade through on that day and then decides
what level of shout to bid or ask in that specialist. For the shout decision, each trader is
endowed with one of four standard automated trading strategies:
• ZI-C: Zero Intelligence—Constrained (Gode and Sunder ), a strategy that
essentially involves random shouting (bidding by potential buyers or asking by
potential sellers) within the budget constraint of each trader. This strategy ignores
any trading history or experience of the trader.
• ZIP: Zero Intelligence Plus (Cliff and Bruten ), a strategy that takes account
of the trader’s experience to extend ZI-C and adapts the shouting price according
to changing market conditions.
• RE: Roth and Erev (Erev and Roth ), a strategy that mimics reinforcement
learning by humans in game-playing.
• GD: Gjerstad-Dickhaut (Gjerstad and Dickhaut ), a strategy in which traders
form beliefs about the expected success and profits from particular shouts based
on their trading experience.
These strategies were selected because they have been extensively studied in the
automated trading literature, and some have also been shown to work well in practice.
Within the CAT Tournament, the strategy used by each trader is private knowledge,
andisnotrevealedtoothertradersnortothespecialists.Also,theproportionoftraders
executing each of the four strategies is not revealed to specialists.the cat market design competition 473
Each trading day in the CAT Tournament begins with specialists deciding on and
posting their fee levels for all traders to see. The fee structure and fee levels inform the
traders’ decisions as to which specialist to select that day. Specialists have the following
goals:
• To attract traders to their marketplace, in competition with the other specialists;
• To match potential buyers with potential sellers through a market matching and
clearing algorithm; and
• To earn profits by deciding a daily fee structure and fee levels, such as fees for
placing a shout or a commission fee based on a trader’s profit.
Entrants to the tournament are scored on three equally weighted criteria each
trading day: share of all profits earned by specialists that day, share of traders attracted
to their marketplace that day, and the specialists’ transaction success rate, which is
the percentage of traders that were successfully matched with counterparties by the
specialist. These daily scores are summed over the course of the tournament, with
the winner being that specialist having the highest cumulative score across all scored
days. Toeliminate thepossibility ofspecialists’ takingtacticaladvantageofedgeeffects,
scoring in the tournament does not commence until some days after the first trading
day, and ends some days before the last trading day.
## 16.2.3 History of the Tournament: –
The CAT Market Design Tournament was run five times, once each year from  to
. The tournament was operated as part of the annual Trading Agent Competitions
(TAC), hosted each northern summer by the International Trading Agent Research
Association. The first TAC game, now called TAC Classic,invited entrantsto program
trading agents able to buy and sell various electronic goods in multiple complementary
marketplaces. The name CAT was adopted for the Market Design Competition for two
reasons: first, because it is short for catallactics, the science of economic exchange,
and second, because the game operates in reverse to the way in which TAC Classic
operates: in CAT, the entrants provide marketplaces and the competition organizers
provide automated traders, rather than the reverse.
The TAC Competitions are usually held alongside a leading computer science
research conference in artificial intelligence, multiagent systems, or e-commerce, and
so they change location each year. The CAT Tournament was hosted in Vancouver,
Canada (), Chicago (), Pasadena, California, (), Boston () and
Barcelona (). The games in , , and  were operated from a server in
the Department of Computer Science at the University of Liverpool, UK, while those

## 16.3.1 Modeling Market Mechanisms
Niu et al. () presented a modular model of market mechanisms in preparing a
reference implementation of market mechanism for entrants of the CAT Tournaments.
In this modular view, which extends prior understandings of market mechanisms (e.g.,
Wurman et al. ), a market mechanism is composed of multiple auction rules, or
whattheycalledpolicies,eachregulatingoneaspectofthemarketplace.Thereareseven
different types of policy:
. matching policies define how a market matches shouts made by traders;
. quote policies determine the quotes issued by markets;
. shout accepting policies judge whether a shout made by a trader should be
permitted in the market;
. clearingpoliciesdefinewhentoclearthemarketandexecutetransactionsbetween
matched asks and bids;
. pricing policies set transaction prices for matched ask-bid pairs;
. charging policies determine the charges imposed by a market; and
. subscribingpoliciescontrolthecollectionofmarketinformationsothatthemarket
mechanism may adapt itself.
A more detailed description of this model and numerous policies that can be
classified in such a way and are implemented in JCAT are given by Niu ().
According to the entries that were uploaded into the TAC repository, this modular
model was generally adopted by the entrants of the CAT tournaments, and the policies
in JCAT were the primitive building blocks for the entrants to design more advanced
components of their market mechanisms.
Forexample,acommonshoutacceptingpolicyiswhatNiu()callsaquote-beating
acceptingpolicy(alsoknownastheNYSEshoutimprovementruleowingtoitsusebythe
NewYorkStockExchange).Thispolicyistypicallyusedinthecontinuousdoubleauction
(CDA), where traders may submit shouts at any time during trading, transactions are
executed whenever a pair of shouts can be matched, and a shout is allowed to be
placed in the market only when it is more competitive than the corresponding market476 tim miller et al.
quotes; that is, proposed asks need to be lower than the ask quote, and proposed bids
need to be higher than the bid quote. The market quotes are typically determined by
the least-competitive matched shout from the opposite side and the most-competitive
unmatched shout from the same side for example, the ask quote being based on
the lowest matched bid and the lowest unmatched ask (McCabe et al. ). The
quote-beating policy is believed effective in speeding up the convergence to the market
competitiveequilibriuminaCDAmarket(CliffandBruten).Althoughthispolicy
issimpleandcanbeeasilyunderstoodbyhumantradersintraditionalmarkets,itrelies
upon limited information and may lead to volatile transaction prices when traders are
sub-rational and the shouts they place do not cluster around the market competitive
equilibrium price. In fact, the market quotes can be viewed as estimates of the market
competitive equilibrium price, the ask quote being the upper bound and the bid quote
being the lower bound.
Niu et al. () proposed what they called the equilibrium-beating accepting policy
using the average of transaction prices in a sliding window of the transaction history as
the estimated equilibrium price. They showed that this simple method was effective in
reducingpricefluctuationsaswellasimprovingtheallocativeefficiencyinastand-alone
CDA market populated by ZI-C traders.
Various CAT entries devised their variants to obtain desirable results in the CAT
setting. PersianCat in CAT  (Honari et al. ), for instance, estimated the
market equilibrium price with a running average of the minimum price of matched
bids and the maximum price of matched asks on each day over a certain number of
recent game days. This variant of equilibrium estimation samples from a relatively long
history of transactions and helps maintain an even smoother estimate over time. An
improvedversionofAstonCATinCAT(Changetal.)combinedtheoriginal
equilibrium-beating accepting policy and the PersianCat variant in a linear manner,
where the weighted parameters were carefully chosen to balance the information
learnedfromtheintradaytradingaswellastradingspanningmultipledays.PersianCat
won the  CAT tournament and the improved AstonCAT, or AstonCAT-plus,

The designers of both PersianCat  and AstonCAT-plus attributed their specialist’s

migrated between marketplaces as the entries interacted and adapted their strategies

in an ecological process in which highly rewarded actions became more and more

ecological evolution of entries in the Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma Tournament of

in varying competitive environments. For example, IAMwildCAT, the CAT 
champion, could lose the competition against PersianCat through one-on-one games
in certain experimental setups. Indeed, the actual tournaments reflected only limited
